title: Processes, Threads and Scheduling
objectives: Explain what a process and a thread are, and exactly what each shares or owns
Describe the stages of a context switch and quantify its direct and indirect costs
Predict worst-case scheduling delay for a given thread count, core count and time slice
Relate scheduling jitter and preemption to tail latency in trading systems
motivation: Your strategy process just got preempted mid-tick and the fill arrived 400 microseconds late. No amount of algorithmic cleverness fixes that: the operating system, not your code, decided who ran on the CPU. Understanding processes, threads and the scheduler is the difference between a backtest that says 10 microseconds and production that says 60.

blocks.md: A **process** is a program in execution: the kernel gives it a private virtual address space, its own file-descriptor table, credentials and a process ID (PID). A **thread** is the unit the scheduler actually runs. Every process starts with one thread; adding threads via pthread_create or std::thread gives each new thread its own stack, register set and thread-local storage, while everything else, heap, globals, open files, signal dispositions, stays shared. That split explains both the appeal and the danger of threads: sharing memory makes communication nearly free, and makes corruption easy.

blocks.md: The layout above is the map every address in your process resolves against. Threads of the same process see exactly this map, same text, same heap, differing only in stack and TLS. A second *process* (created by fork) gets a private copy of the mapping; pages are not physically copied until one side writes (copy-on-write), so fork is cheap to issue but expensive the moment either side starts writing heavily.

blocks.text: Context switches: what they cost and why

blocks.md: A **context switch** is the kernel suspending one task and resuming another: save the old task's registers into its control block, load the next task's, switch the memory-map if the new task is a different process (invalidating TLB entries for the old address space), and jump back to user mode. The direct cost is a microsecond or two. The indirect cost, cold L1/L2 cache and TLB lines, because the new task touches different memory, is often several times worse. Two threads of one process switch cheaper: no address-space change, no TLB flush.

blocks.title: Worked example: preemption vs a latency budget
items: Hot-path budget: 20 microseconds from market-data event to order. One involuntary preemption happens on average once every 2,000 events; each costs an effective 6 microseconds (direct switch plus cache refill).
Average cost per event: $6\,\mu s / 2{,}000 = 3\,\text{ns}$ - invisible in the mean.
But the unlucky event pays the full 6 microseconds: $6 / 20 = 30\%$ of the entire budget, gone.
Desks therefore optimise the *tail*: pin hot threads to isolated cores, raise priorities, or busy-spin so the scheduler never interrupts at all.

blocks.title: Tail latency is a scheduling problem
blocks.md: A backtest measures your strategy; the scheduler decides whether production matches it. A 12 ms scheduling delay on a \$5M order is 12 ms of unapproved risk. CPU pinning (sched_setaffinity), core isolation and real-time scheduling exist so that the 99.9th percentile, not the average, stays inside budget. A desk that only measures the mean will ship a system that works beautifully except when it matters.

The kernel keeps runnable tasks on a runqueue. On Linux the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) picks the runnable task with the least *virtual runtime*; nice values weight the choice, and the real-time classes (SCHED_FIFO, SCHED_RR) preempt everything else. Each task gets a **time slice**; when the slice expires, or the task blocks on I/O or a lock, the scheduler runs someone else. Blocked tasks cost nothing; *runnable but waiting* tasks are where latency comes from.

blocks.title: Worked example: worst-case delay under round-robin
items: Setup: 16 runnable threads, 4 cores, slice = 3 ms.
One full round requires $16 \times 3 = 48$ ms of CPU time.
Spread over 4 cores: $48 / 4 = 12$ ms of wall-clock time per round.
So any thread can be forced to wait up to about **12 ms** between turns, at trading scale an eternity: light crosses the Atlantic in roughly 30 ms.

blocks.md: Threads bring their own arithmetic. Linux reserves 8 MiB of *virtual* address space per thread stack by default, usually almost untouched, so resident memory stays small, but 10,000 threads still commit 80 GiB of address space plus kernel-side bookkeeping per thread. Oversubscription (runnable threads far above the core count) turns every slice expiry into a switch; the fix is thread pools sized to the workload, spinning instead of sleeping on the hottest paths, and affinity so a thread's cache stays warm.

items: Involuntary preemption at slice expiry, mitigate with affinity, isolation and RT priorities.
Voluntary blocking on I/O or a contended lock, mitigate by reducing sharing or wait time.
Interrupt handling landing on your core (NIC, timer), steer IRQs elsewhere.

blocks.caption: Build with -pthread. slot_id is private to each thread even though both share the process heap, the distinction this whole lesson hangs on.

guidedExercise.prompt: A hot-path handler has a budget of 20 microseconds per event. Preemptions strike on average once every 2,000 events and each costs an effective 6 microseconds. (a) Compute the *average* added latency per event in nanoseconds. (b) Compute the added latency on the preemption event as a percentage of the budget. (c) Say which of (a) or (b) justifies CPU pinning, and why.
hints: Average = per-event cost divided by the event interval.
6 microseconds out of a 20 microsecond budget is what fraction?
guidedExercise.solution: (a) $6\,\mu s / 2{,}000 = 0.003\,\mu s = 3$ ns per event, undetectable in the mean. (b) $6 / 20 = 30\%$ of the budget consumed by one unlucky event. (c) Only (b) matters for trading: pinning trades a little throughput for a collapsed tail, which is exactly what a latency budget cares about.

independentExercise.prompt: A service runs on 6 cores with 42 runnable threads under round-robin, slice 5 ms. (a) Compute the worst-case scheduling delay in ms. (b) The team cuts to 12 threads by moving background work to another machine; recompute. (c) Name one further mitigation and its trade-off.
hints: 42 x 5 = 210 ms of CPU work per round.
independentExercise.solution: (a) $42 \times 5 / 6 = 35$ ms. (b) $12 \times 5 / 6 = 10$ ms. (c) Pin the remaining threads (better cache locality, less scheduling flexibility), or spin instead of sleeping on isolated cores (burns CPU for latency).

commonMistakes: Equating threads with speed: beyond the core count, extra runnable threads mostly buy context switches, not parallelism.
Reading a thread's 8 MiB stack reservation as real memory use, it is virtual; RSS is what counts.
Assuming fork() copies the whole address space up front, pages are shared copy-on-write until someone writes.
Counting only the register-save cost of a context switch and ignoring the cache/TLB refill that usually dominates.
realWorldApplication: Every container orchestrator, database and network server lives under this scheduler; sizing thread pools and interpreting runqueue statistics are exactly this lesson's arithmetic.
quantFinanceApplication: Feed handlers and order gateways are built around these numbers: preemption cost vs tick budget, worst-case round-robin delay, and core pinning to keep the 99.9th percentile fill latency inside the firm's risk limits.
summary: Processes own private address spaces; threads own stacks, registers and TLS, and share everything else in the address space.
A context switch has a direct cost (~1-2 microseconds) and an often larger indirect cost from cold caches and TLB entries.
Worst-case round-robin delay = (runnable threads x slice) / cores: 16 threads on 4 cores with 3 ms slices means up to 12 ms of waiting.
Trading systems manage the tail, not the mean: pinning, core isolation and spinning exist to remove scheduler-induced jitter.

quiz.prompt: Two threads of the same process are running. Which resource does each thread own privately?
quiz.explanation: Threads share the address space (heap, globals) and the file-descriptor table; the kernel gives each thread its own stack, register context and thread-local storage.

quiz.prompt: 16 runnable threads share 4 cores under round-robin with a 3 ms slice. What is the approximate worst-case delay, in ms, before a ready thread runs again?
quiz.explanation: One round is 16 x 3 = 48 ms of CPU time; over 4 cores that is 48/4 = 12 ms of wall-clock time, so a thread may wait up to about 12 ms between turns.

quiz.prompt: Why is a switch between two threads of the *same* process cheaper than a switch between two different processes?
options: The page tables do not change, so the TLB is not flushed
quiz.explanation: Threads share one address space, so the memory-map switch (and its TLB invalidation) disappears. Registers still get saved and restored, and threads still block.

quiz.prompt: list.append is atomic under the GIL in CPython. What does this script print?
quiz.explanation: Each of the two threads appends exactly 3 elements and append is atomic, so every append lands: 2 x 3 = 6. Replace append with data = data + [x] and the interleaving races appear.

quiz.prompt: Which actions genuinely reduce scheduling-induced tail latency for a hot trading thread?
options: Pin the thread to a CPU isolated from the general scheduler
Raise the number of runnable threads above the core count
Set the hot thread's nice value to +19 (lowest priority)
Busy-spin on an isolated core instead of sleeping between events
Steer NIC interrupts onto a different core than the hot thread
quiz.explanation: +19 demotes the thread behind every other task, and oversubscription multiplies switches. Pinning, spinning on isolated cores and moving IRQs away all keep the hot path uninterrupted.

quiz.prompt: In one or two sentences: what is preemption, and when does the kernel perform it?
quiz.modelAnswer: Preemption is the kernel forcibly suspending a running task, typically when its time slice expires or a higher-priority task becomes runnable, saving its state so it can resume later.
quiz.explanation: Preemption is involuntary scheduling: the task did not block or exit, the kernel took the CPU back, usually on a timer interrupt or a wake-up of a higher-priority task.

flashcards.back: A process owns a private virtual address space, FD table and PID; threads are the schedulable units inside it, each with a private stack/registers/TLS but sharing heap, globals and open files.
$t_{\text{wait}} \approx \dfrac{N_{\text{runnable}} \times \text{slice}}{N_{\text{cores}}}$ - e.g. 16 threads x 3 ms slice / 4 cores = 12 ms.
Direct: register save/restore + mode switch (~1-2 microseconds). Indirect: cold caches/TLB afterwards, often several times worse, the part that hurts tail latency.

flashcards.front: Why do desks pin threads and isolate cores?
flashcards.back: To keep p99.9 latency stable: no involuntary preemption, warm caches, no IRQ interference. The mean barely changes but the tail collapses.
